newsitem.title: USA: NYS Assembly wants level welfare benefits - source.
newsitem.headline: NYS Assembly wants level welfare benefits - source.

text.p: The New York State Assembly, which started putting out its welfare plan, rejected the sliding benefit cuts proposed by Gov George Pataki, a legislative source said on Wednesday.
A new federal program enacted last August poses a big challenge for New York State as its constitution obliges it to care for the needy.

The legislative source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said that the Assembly plan, still being fine-tuned, had three main programs. The proposal by Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, would soften the new federal welfare program.

"What he (Silver) tried to do was to take the best out of what Washington did and move welfare from a generational dependency program to transitional assistance," said the source, adding the Assembly expected to approve its welfare bill by early next week.
A spokesman for the Republican governor was not immediately available to comment.
But the Democrat-led Assembly would impose work requirements -- a major part of the governor's plan -- though it would not exclude education.

"Everyone must work," said the source, explaining that people would lose their benefits unless they had done everything they could to find jobs. Those individuals would qualify for a safety net program.
The Assembly's new program would use a federal grant -- approximately $2.4 billion during the first year -- to give families benefits for five years. "There are no grant cuts," the source said.
The second feature of the Assembly's program, a safety net, would give counties the option of using a restricted cash program with a modified voucher system.

Local administrators would give welfare recipients rent checks, which could not be cashed, to give to their landlords. Utilities could be paid directly, while the recipients could charge the rest of the benefits on a debit card. They would be able to withdraw about 20 percent as cash, the source said.
Pataki's safety net program called for noncash vouchers, a method criticized by localities for imposing administrative costs and increasing the system's complexity.

Under the third part of the Assembly's plan, single, able-bodied adults, who were covered by the former state Home Relief program, would qualify for a two-year plan that Albany would fund. After that period, they would be eligible for the safety net if they could not find jobs.

People who were disabled would have to work unless their physicians decided they could not, the source said. Legal immigrants would receive benefits, and the Assembly would spend another $5 million on a program to help them become citizens.
The Assembly would define work more broadly than Pataki, including on-the-job-training, workfare, vocational education and education, the source said.

The only individuals who would be exempt from the work requirement would be new mothers, who would not have to work for three months. Childcare would be available for parents whose children who were under age 13, the source added.
